newsitem.title: USA: Money growth creates inflation-St Louis Fed Melzer. [CORRECTED 16:28 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Money growth creates inflation-St Louis Fed Melzer. [CORRECTED 16:28 GMT]

text.p: Rapid money growth -- and not economic growth -- is responsible for inflation, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis President Thomas (corrects name from Louis) Melzer said on Wednesday.
"I want to stress that economic growth does not cause inflation," Melzer told an Arkansas State Bank Department's conference in Hot Springs, Ark. The speech was made available in New York.
"Persistently high rates of money growth, however you define them, translate into persistently high rates of inflation," Melzer stated.
Melzer explained persistent inflation arises where the "prices of goods and services can all rise at once if the amount of currency in circulation is expanded enough."
"Thus, monetary system can produce inflation," the St. Louis Fed president pointed out. "This is the basis for the assertion that inflation is a monetary phenomenon."

While admitting that prices can undergo spikes and temporarily affect the economy, Melzer stressed "temporary inflation is by its very definition less of a concern to monetary policymakers. If it is temporary, it will dissipate on its own accord and requires no policy action."
Melzer said the United States was "lucky... to have had inflation of around 3.0 percent for nearly the whole of the current expansion."
"But this 3.0 percent is an entrenched, monetarily-induced inflation which is not going to go away unless the Fed takes specific action to eliminate it," Melzer stressed.

Echoing a defense of the Fed's preemptive policy that Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan presented last month, Melzer admitted "Of course, taking action to move the monetary inflation rate lower is controversial."
Melzer, responding to "many of the Fed's critics... that the Fed has been excessively concerned about inflation during the current expansion," said "they are missing the point."

"The more successful policy involves watching inflation trends carefully and acting preemptively to stave off incipient inflationary pressures," Melzer added. "The success of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC)'s policy has been that the Fed has moved with enough agility to keep inflation at bay."
The St. Louis Fed president also reiterated the Fed is not anti-jobs or anti-growth.
